headline_marked: [[Valar Atomics activates nuclear microreactor]] live, powering an Nvidia RTX PC on stage
headline: Valar Atomics activates nuclear microreactor live, powering an Nvidia RTX PC on stage
summary: Valar Atomics partnered with Nvidia to build a 30MW closed-loop AI factory, demonstrating their Ward 250 microreactor by powering an Nvidia RTX desktop and a website.
details: Valar Atomics successfully activated its Ward 250 nuclear microreactor live on stage, announcing a partnership with Nvidia. During the event, an Nvidia RTX desktop unit was plugged into the reactor, which was then turned up to 37% power to activate the Blackwell-powered PC. The company also demonstrated that its "nuclearwebsite.com" page is solely run from a server powered by this reactor.

CEO Isiah Taylor explained the process: uranium atoms fission inside the reactor, producing 100 kilowatts of thermal energy. This energy is extracted by a pressurized helium cooling loop, and the hot helium flows into a thermal electric generator (TEG), creating the electrical current that powers the Nvidia chip and the website.

While Valar Atomics claims to be the first startup to achieve power production, the Department of Energy notes two other firms, Deployable Energy and Antares Nuclear, have also reached criticality with small modular reactors (SMRs). Major tech giants like Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Oracle have invested in nuclear technologies since 2024, anticipating massive power demands from AI data centers.

The increasing power and water consumption of AI data centers has become a significant national issue, leading to public pushback and increased utility costs. This resistance has resulted in the delay or cancellation of at least 75 data center projects in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

This public and governmental pressure is driving innovation in both private and public sectors. SMRs aim to meet electricity demands without straining national grids, while companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Nvidia are developing technologies to reduce data center water use by up to 100%.

headline_marked: [[Z.ai launches ZCode]], an agent-first AI coding environment for GLM-5.2
headline: Z.ai launches ZCode, an agent-first AI coding environment for GLM-5.2
summary: Z.ai's new desktop app, ZCode, is an "Agentic Development Environment" for its GLM-5.2 model, challenging rivals like GitHub Copilot. It offers unique remote control via popular messaging apps.
details: Z.ai, formerly Zhipu AI, has officially launched ZCode, a free desktop application designed as an "Agentic Development Environment" for its flagship GLM-5.2 large language model. This move positions ZCode directly against established AI coding tools like Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot.
Available on macOS, Windows, and Linux, ZCode supports bring-your-own-key (BYOK) configurations for third-party models. Subscribers to Z.ai's GLM Coding Plan also receive a 1.5x usage-quota bonus.

Unlike traditional IDEs that add AI features, ZCode is built as an agent-first environment, focusing on long-horizon tasks. Users describe an outcome, and the ZCode Agent plans, edits files, runs checks, and iterates until the goal is met.

The development experience is organized around the ZCode Agent, deeply tuned for GLM-5.2, ensuring deep integration of the model, tools, and execution workflow. This allows for continuous, multi-step real-world development tasks.

A key differentiator is the remote-control feature, enabling users to steer running coding agents from WeChat, Feishu, or Telegram on their phones. This feature is particularly tailored for the Chinese developer market, where these messaging platforms are dominant.

The ZCode tool is free to download, with revenue generated through Z.ai's GLM Coding Plan subscriptions. Plans start at $16.20 per month for "Lite" and go up to $144 per month for "Max," significantly undercutting competitors like Anthropic's Claude Code.

ZCode also pragmatically supports multiple AI models and agents, including Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and OpenCode, recognizing that no single model excels at every task. A promotional 1.5x effective quota bonus is offered through July 31 for Coding Plan subscribers.

The platform showcases GLM-5.2, a formidable 744-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts architecture with 40 billion active parameters and a one-million-token context window. It was trained on 28.5 trillion tokens and ranked second globally on Code Arena.

Notably, GLM-5.2 was developed entirely without American chips, running on Huawei silicon, with estimated training costs around $25 million. This makes it an extraordinarily cost-effective model compared to Western frontier models.
